title: Hx2Dx: From Anamnesis to Diagnosis - A Multimodal Arena for Conversational Clinical Reasoning in LLMs
authors: Federico Ravenda, Mirko Cesarini, Daniele Montagnani, Volodymyr Karpenko, Antonietta Mira, Andrea Raballo
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve expert-level diagnostic accuracy in static evaluations, where the model receives a curated vignette or case report that already condenses the diagnostically relevant findings. Such evaluations measure inference over already selected evidence; the evaluations do not account for the inquiry used to obtain it. In clinical practice, however, diagnosis is an iterative process of inquiry. Clinicians take the patient's history, or anamnesis (Hx), through targeted questioning, examine the patient, and request and interpret tests, progressively narrowing the differential until they reach a final diagnosis (Dx). We introduce Hx2Dx ARENA, an interactive benchmark of 1'000 clinical cases from the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM). Each case is a simulated encounter that proceeds from initial presentation through history taking and physical examination to diagnostic workup. We evaluate open- and closed-source LLMs under multiple configurations. Performance varies considerably across models in the interactive setting, and every model loses diagnostic accuracy relative to the static setting, where the full case is presented upfront. The ability to ask the right questions accounts for much of both the gap between models and the loss of accuracy: diagnosis improves as questions become more targeted and build a more complete clinical picture. LLMs thus reason well once the relevant data are available but remain limited in hypothesis-driven information gathering, in knowing what to ask in order to know. Closing this gap is a prerequisite for their safe integration into real-world diagnostic workflows.

infographic.key_insight: LLMs lose diagnostic accuracy when they must gather clinical information interactively rather than receive the full case upfront.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Assessing how models ask questions—not just interpret supplied findings—is important before considering real-world diagnostic use.
method: Introduced Hx2Dx ARENA with 1,000 simulated clinical encounters drawn from NEJM cases.
Modeled history taking, physical examination, and diagnostic workup.
Evaluated open- and closed-source LLMs across configurations and compared interactive with static performance.
infographic.evidence_signal: Every evaluated model performed worse interactively than with full-case input, while more targeted questioning and a more complete clinical picture were associated with better diagnosis.
infographic.watch_item: Performance on simulated, publication-derived cases does not establish safety or effectiveness in real clinical encounters.
infographic.paper_title: Hx2Dx: From Anamnesis to Diagnosis - A Multimodal Arena for Conversational Clinical Reasoning in LLMs

title: The BRIDGE dataset: paired brightfield whole-slide images of prostate core-needle biopsies in paraffin, after deparaffinization and H&E staining
authors: Julia A. Mielcarz, Justyna Durślewicz, Marek Zdrenka, Ahmad Abbadi, Martin Eklund, Mateusz Matusiak
abstract: Computational approaches are increasingly being explored to streamline histopathology workflows, including label-free methods that aim to reduce reliance on chemical staining. Among these, deep learning-based label-free virtual staining uses images of unstained tissue to computationally generate stained images. Despite growing interest, model development and validation remain constrained by the scarcity of paired, clinically annotated whole-slide imaging datasets. We present BRIDGE, a dataset of prostate core-needle biopsies collected at the Prof. Franciszek Lukaszczyk Oncology Centre in Bydgoszcz, Poland. The dataset comprises 869 glass slides from 169 patients, each digitized sequentially after sectioning, deparaffinization, and hematoxylin and eosin staining, yielding in total 2607 whole-slide images. The dataset supports the development and external validation of label-free virtual staining, virtual unstaining, image-registration and segmentation methods. Each slide is accompanied by a Gleason score, enabling downstream analyses of cancer classification and grading concordance. The stained images can be used independently for color normalization and cross-scanner robustness studies. All images are de-identified, distributed in their native scanner format and will be available through the BioImage Archive.

infographic.key_insight: BRIDGE provides paired prostate biopsy whole-slide images across three preparation stages to support AI research in label-free virtual staining and related tasks.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The dataset could support research on reducing reliance on chemical staining and evaluating cancer grading concordance, but clinical performance is not established here.
method: Digitized each slide sequentially in paraffin, after deparaffinization, and after H&E staining.
Paired images across preparation stages and provided slide-level Gleason scores.
De-identified images in native scanner format for planned release through BioImage Archive.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 2,607 whole-slide images from 869 slides and 169 patients at one Polish oncology centre, without model performance results.
infographic.watch_item: Single-centre sourcing may limit generalizability; models developed using BRIDGE require independent validation.
infographic.paper_title: The BRIDGE dataset: paired brightfield whole-slide images of prostate core-needle biopsies in paraffin, after deparaffinization and H&E staining

title: TrialDesignBench: Benchmarking Language Models for Phase-I Trial Design Against Clinical Knowledge
authors: Yihan Hank Tang, Peng Yang, Jiayi Xin, Tianqi Shang, Xuyang Chen, Ying Yuan
abstract: AI is used in much of the clinical trial pipeline. However, selecting the statistical design of a trial, a crucial step that determines how drug doses are tested on humans and evaluated, has seen almost no AI progress. LLMs appear to be a natural fit given their strengths in biomedical knowledge and statistical reasoning. Nevertheless, there is currently no appropriate way to evaluate such abilities because recent regulatory and methodological shifts, most notably FDA's Project Optimus, have redefined what constitutes a reasonable design and rendered many previous designs obsolete. To lay the groundwork for AI-assisted trial design, we introduce TrialDesignBench, a benchmark of 617 Phase-I/I-II oncology dose-finding trials, each paired with an expert-validated reference design that is consistent with the latest FDA regulatory initiatives. This reference standard is produced through a formalization of the expert design process. We evaluate five frontier LLMs, none of which matches the reference standard. Our ablation experiments trace this performance gap to two main causes, inference of latent, unrecorded design determinants from trial sources (supplying them raises class-wise balanced accuracy by 0.22) and structured decision-tree reasoning (+0.24). TrialDesignBench offers a reproducible, contemporary-standard objective for evaluating and enhancing AI-assisted trial design.

infographic.key_insight: TrialDesignBench reveals a gap between frontier LLMs and expert-validated, contemporary standards for early-phase oncology trial design.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The benchmark could support research toward AI-assisted dose-finding trial design aligned with recent FDA initiatives, including Project Optimus.
method: Compiled 617 Phase-I/I-II oncology dose-finding trials.
Paired trials with expert-validated reference designs using a formalized expert decision process.
Evaluated five frontier LLMs and tested sources of performance gaps through ablations.
infographic.evidence_signal: None of the five LLMs matched the reference standard; supplying latent design determinants increased class-wise balanced accuracy by 0.22, while structured decision-tree reasoning increased it by 0.24.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark performance does not establish prospective clinical utility, and important design determinants may be missing from trial records.
infographic.paper_title: TrialDesignBench: Benchmarking Language Models for Phase-I Trial Design Against Clinical Knowledge

title: BioMem: Agentic Memory for Biomedical LLM Agents
authors: Mingchen Li, Yongkang Xiao, Rumeng Li, Rui Zhang, Hong Yu
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential in biomedical applications, while agentic memory systems have emerged as a promising approach to preserving and utilizing information across tasks and interactions. However, a fundamental question remains: how effectively and reliably do these systems retain, retrieve, update, and utilize biomedical information? In this study, we systematically investigate agentic memory in the biomedical domain, focusing on task effectiveness, retrieval quality, information fidelity, and long-term robustness. We evaluate five memory approaches across four LLMs in three representative settings: biomedical knowledge reasoning, clinical prediction, and long-term conversational memory. Our analyses reveal how memory construction, evidence relevance, and conversational history shape downstream biomedical performance, highlighting the distinct challenges of retrieving relevant information, preserving its fidelity, and effectively utilizing it for reasoning. Building on these findings, we introduce Hybrid Memory Retrieval and Utilization (HMRU), a training-free framework that jointly enhances evidence accessibility and task-aware utilization to improve biomedical reasoning and long-term conversational memory. HMRU achieves an average relative improvement of 8.6% across biomedical question-answering and conversational memory benchmarks, with additional gains in selected clinical prediction tasks. It further reduces conversational answer errors by 24.9% and closes 48.0% of the performance gap to full-context inference. Our findings provide a systematic characterization of biomedical agentic memory and practical insights into developing more effective and reliable memory-augmented LLM systems.

infographic.key_insight: BioMem introduces HMRU, a training-free framework that improves how biomedical LLM agents retrieve and use stored information.
infographic.clinical_relevance: More reliable memory could support biomedical reasoning and clinical prediction, but these benchmark findings do not establish safety or benefit in patient care.
method: Evaluated five memory approaches across four LLMs.
Tested biomedical knowledge reasoning, clinical prediction, and long-term conversational memory.
Developed HMRU to improve evidence accessibility and task-aware use.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an average relative improvement of 8.6% across biomedical QA and conversational memory benchmarks, 24.9% fewer conversational answer errors, and closure of 48.0% of the gap to full-context inference.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark gains do not guarantee reliable clinical deployment; retrieved information must remain relevant, faithful, and current.
infographic.paper_title: BioMem: Agentic Memory for Biomedical LLM Agents

title: An evidence-traceable benchmark of clinical reasoning in large language models
authors: Zhiqun Zhao, Xiaodong Yang, Bruce Gu, Ming Li, Yi Fu, Song Li
abstract: Benchmark scores for medical large language models (LLMs) are difficult to interpret when scoring criteria cannot be traced to clinical evidence. Here we developed Med Evidence Bench (MEB; https://www.medevidencebench.org.cn/), comprising 1,536 physician-constructed items across three levels: guideline knowledge, standardized clinical scenarios and real-world laboratory scenarios. Each criterion stating a medical claim is linked to a versioned source-text span. Across ten LLMs, the Evidence Trace Score (ETS) was 0.975-0.997 for guideline knowledge, 0.292-0.658 for standardized scenarios and 0.182-0.447 for real-world scenarios, and rankings varied across levels. For real-world scenarios, scores for identifying clinical information (mean, 0.770) exceeded those for matching evidence (0.165) or formulating recommendations (0.160). On 1,296 criterion-level judgments, automated grading agreed with the majority vote of three physicians (macro-F1, 0.930; 95% confidence interval, 0.915-0.945), although agreement was lower for evidence application. These findings from Chinese-language materials indicate that guideline recall does not ensure patient-specific evidence use and do not establish clinical effectiveness.

infographic.key_insight: Strong guideline recall did not translate into patient-specific evidence use across ten medical LLMs.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Medical LLM evaluation should test evidence application in clinical scenarios, not just guideline knowledge.
method: Built Med Evidence Bench with 1,536 physician-constructed Chinese-language items.
Tested guideline knowledge, standardized clinical scenarios and real-world laboratory scenarios.
Linked each medical-claim scoring criterion to a versioned source-text span.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across ten LLMs, Evidence Trace Scores fell from 0.975–0.997 for guideline knowledge to 0.182–0.447 for real-world scenarios; automated grading achieved macro-F1 0.930 against physician-majority judgments.
infographic.watch_item: Findings from Chinese-language materials do not establish clinical effectiveness, and automated grading agreement was lower for evidence application.
infographic.paper_title: An evidence-traceable benchmark of clinical reasoning in large language models

title: Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System for ICU Discharge Risk Assessment
authors: Guoqing Zhang, Rafik Hadfi, Takayuki Ito
abstract: Unplanned 30-day intensive care unit (ICU) readmission is a critical benchmark for evaluating healthcare quality. Most predictive models assume readmission risk depends solely on a patient's individual pathophysiological state, ignoring hospital operational context and resource capacity. In practice, discharge decisions are dynamic trade-offs between patient stability and bed turnover pressures. To address this gap, we develop an Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) for ICU discharge risk assessment. The system combines multi-agent collaborative extraction with self-evolving retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to eliminate template noise from progress notes, while constructing departmental workload indicators alongside admission flow features, continuous vital signs, and sparse medical codes (ICD/DRG). Addressing severe class imbalance (about 10.5% readmissions) and alarm fatigue, we implement data normalization, class reweighting, and decision-threshold calibration. In 20 independent runs across 20,000 ICU stays from MIMIC-III, empirical findings demonstrate that: vital signs alone have limited predictive capacity under real-world class imbalance (PR-AUC of 0.1387 +/- 0.0086); directly concatenating raw text embeddings degrades decision tree performance (XGBoost and LightGBM PR-AUC drop to 0.3893 and 0.4030); whereas an end-to-end multimodal fine-tuning architecture (Transformer E2E FineTune) utilizing layer-wise parameter freezing and differential learning rates reverses text negative transfer, achieving the highest AUROC of 0.8288 +/- 0.0110, PR-AUC of 0.4373 +/- 0.0310, and F1-Score of 0.4757 +/- 0.0196. Operational indicators supply independent risk signals, laying an engineering foundation for high-utility clinical decision support tools.

infographic.key_insight: An operation-aware multimodal model combining patient data, clinical notes, and hospital workload signals achieved the strongest ICU readmission prediction performance among the evaluated approaches.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Accounting for hospital workload alongside patient condition may help contextualize ICU discharge risk, but clinical benefit remains unproven.
method: Combined workload and admission-flow indicators with vital signs, ICD/DRG codes, and clinical notes.
Used multi-agent extraction and self-evolving retrieval-augmented generation to remove note template noise.
Fine-tuned a multimodal Transformer with layer-wise freezing and differential learning rates; addressed imbalance through class reweighting and threshold calibration.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 20 independent runs on 20,000 MIMIC-III ICU stays with approximately 10.5% readmissions, the best model achieved AUROC 0.8288 ± 0.0110, PR-AUC 0.4373 ± 0.0310, and F1 0.4757 ± 0.0196.
infographic.watch_item: Retrospective MIMIC-III results require external and prospective validation before use in discharge decisions.
infographic.paper_title: Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System for ICU Discharge Risk Assessment

title: Domain adaptation of a video Foundation model for Heart Failure Diagnosis from Echocardiography
authors: Mahyar Bolhassani, Tijana Geroski, Narayana S. Singam, Amir Amini
abstract: The rapid advancement of foundation models has transformed computer vision, yet their adaptation to medical imaging, particularly purpose built foundation models for spatio temporal echocardiography videos, remains limited. In this work, we explore the feasibility of fine tuning a pretrained foundation model for video (TimeSformer) for automated diagnosis of reduced ejection fraction heart failure (HFrEF) from apical four chamber videos. The model is finetuned on the publicly available RVENet A4C dataset with a phase aware clip generation strategy that captures complementary systolic and diastolic dynamics. We employ divided space time attention, layer wise learning rate decay, and multi clip inference to enhance robustness under limited data. Experimental results show that full fine tuning of the proposed model outperforms classifier only tuning and a 3D CNN baseline. These findings highlight the potential of leveraging foundation video models for echocardiography based heart failure diagnosis and motivates further domain adaptation studies in medical imaging.

infographic.key_insight: Fully fine-tuning a pretrained TimeSformer video model outperformed classifier-only tuning and a 3D CNN baseline for HFrEF classification from echocardiography.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Video foundation models could support echocardiography-based identification of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, but clinical utility remains unestablished.
method: Fine-tuned TimeSformer on RVENet apical four-chamber echocardiography videos.
Used phase-aware clips to capture complementary systolic and diastolic dynamics.
Applied divided space-time attention, layer-wise learning-rate decay, and multi-clip inference.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on the public RVENet A4C dataset favored full fine-tuning, but the abstract reports no numerical performance metrics or external validation.
infographic.watch_item: Generalizability across clinical sites and patient populations requires external validation before clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: Domain adaptation of a video Foundation model for Heart Failure Diagnosis from Echocardiography

title: Differentiable Inverse Rendering Recovers Intrinsic Properties from Intravascular Optical Coherence Tomography
authors: Ajay Manicka, Karim Kadry, Sebastian Ruiz-Lopera, Maryam Alsharqi, Sanjana Arji, Samuel Ruiperez-Campillo
abstract: Medical images encode intrinsic tissue properties that indicate disease progression, yet these properties remain entangled with the system-dependent physics of image formation. Differentiable inverse rendering asks whether they are recoverable by inverting the imaging system's forward physics rather than through post-hoc correction. We address this in optical coherence tomography (OCT), focusing on the optical attenuation coefficient, a per-pixel marker of pathology and cellular composition. Conventional recovery relies on closed-form inversions limited to simplified light-tissue models, or learned methods coupled to specific imaging configurations. We instead recover per-pixel attenuation from a single OCT image by gradient descent through a differentiable physics-based forward model. We verified the method against analytical solutions, validated it on five in vitro phantoms, and applied it without modification to 29{,}269 clinical intravascular OCT images from 128 patients. The inversion needs no training data or segmentations and is portable across platforms and retrospective archives. Replacing the forward model or recovering another optical parameter leaves the optimization procedure unchanged. We demonstrate per-pixel recovery is tractable because gradient information scales to this high-dimensional problem, where gradient-free methods become intractable. Our work supports quantitative tissue characterization from OCT images and provides a framework for extension across imaging modalities and organ systems.

infographic.key_insight: Differentiable inverse rendering estimates per-pixel optical attenuation from a single OCT image by optimizing through a physics-based image-formation model.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support quantitative tissue characterization in intravascular OCT, but clinical diagnostic benefit remains unestablished.
method: Use a differentiable physics-based forward model of OCT image formation.
Recover per-pixel attenuation through gradient descent without training data or segmentations.
Keep the optimization procedure unchanged when replacing the forward model or target optical parameter.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method was checked against analytical solutions, validated on five in vitro phantoms, and applied without modification to 29,269 clinical intravascular OCT images from 128 patients.
infographic.watch_item: Clinical application does not establish tissue-level accuracy; performance may depend on how well the forward model captures real imaging conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Differentiable Inverse Rendering Recovers Intrinsic Properties from Intravascular Optical Coherence Tomography

title: Ninety-Six Ways to Measure a Scribe: Fragmented Evaluation of Ambient Scribes in Healthcare
authors: Amama Mahmood, Shiye Cao, Laura Fleig, Junan Jiang, Theodore Jensen, Yee-Yin Choong
abstract: Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes have moved rapidly from experimental pilots to enterprise-wide deployment across health systems, promising reduced documentation burden and improved clinician experience. While research evaluating these tools has expanded quickly, there are no agreed-upon protocols or standardized metrics for assessing their performance, making it difficult to compare findings or cumulatively synthesize evidence across studies. Across 54 recent evaluation studies, we identify ten evaluation dimensions and 40 distinct metrics, operationalized in 96 different ways-35 of them (36%) used by only a single study. Assessment is dominated by documentation efficiency and time, measured in 44 of 54 studies. The other dimensions appear at broadly similar rates (16-24 studies each), and safety and clinical outcome least consistently of all. Ripple effects on the broader care system, such as impact on patients' care outcomes, redistribution of work, changes in billing and coding intensity, and downstream use of notes by other clinicians are rarely assessed. Moreover, the metrics used rely heavily on self-report and are fragmented and inconsistently operationalized, which limits comparability and hinders synthesis across studies. As an effort to support more rigorous and cumulative evaluation, in this paper we review the study designs, data sources, and metrics commonly used to evaluate ambient AI scribes in healthcare settings, discuss the limitations of current evaluation practice, and argue for a more holistic approach grounded in a standardized, multi-dimensional set of metrics.

infographic.key_insight: Ambient AI scribe evaluations use fragmented metrics, limiting comparisons across studies and leaving broader care-system effects underexamined.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Evidence on documentation efficiency should not be assumed to establish benefits for patient outcomes, safety, or team workflows.
method: Reviewed 54 studies evaluating ambient AI scribes in healthcare.
Examined study designs, data sources, and evaluation metrics.
Identified 10 evaluation dimensions, 40 metrics, and 96 operationalizations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Documentation efficiency and time were assessed in 44 of 54 studies, while 35 of 96 metric operationalizations (36%) appeared in only one study.
infographic.watch_item: Heavy reliance on self-report and inconsistent measurement limits evidence synthesis; safety and downstream effects need more systematic evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Ninety-Six Ways to Measure a Scribe: Fragmented Evaluation of Ambient Scribes in Healthcare

title: Weight-Space Programming for Medical Imaging: Do We Still Need Training Data?
authors: Maximilian Lindholz, Richard Ruppel, Annette Milnik, Sebastian Halskov, Semil Eminovic, Charlie A. Hamm
abstract: Can a large language model (LLM) write the parameters of a medical image classifier from medical knowledge alone, without any training data? Such classifiers normally require labelled images, which are costly and often unavailable. We investigate this question through weight-space programming (WSP), in which an LLM writes or adapts the weights and biases of a neural network directly, without optimisation on training data. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra each generate the parameters of a small LeNet-style CNN in a single reply, without tool use and without access to any image. We compare these networks against zero-shot MedSigLIP and against the same architecture trained on labels using the Adam optimiser, across 7 classification tasks in four modalities: chest X-ray, breast ultrasound and abdominal CT (all from MedMNIST), and pelvic MRI (SynthUterus). The LLM-written networks perform above chance on all six MedMNIST tasks, with a mean test AUC of 0.719 for Opus and 0.711 for Astra. Both models outperform MedSigLIP on 5 of 6 tasks while using more than 10,000 times fewer parameters. However, the same network trained with Adam on only 256 labelled images achieves a higher AUC on every MedMNIST task (mean AUC 0.828). On SynthUterus, Opus attains an AUC of 0.764, whereas Astra falls below chance (AUC 0.136) owing to a systematic error. These results show that LLMs can write functional medical classifiers, but that they do not yet replace training data. We release the protocol, logs and all generated weights at https://github.com/MaximilianLindholz/weight-space-programming-medical.

infographic.key_insight: LLMs wrote functional medical image classifiers without seeing images, but training the same architecture on just 256 labelled images performed better.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Weight-space programming may offer a research route for label-scarce medical imaging, but these results do not establish clinical readiness or replace labelled training data.
method: Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra directly generated small LeNet-style CNN weights without images, tools or training-data optimisation.
Evaluated seven classification tasks across chest X-ray, breast ultrasound, abdominal CT and pelvic MRI.
Compared against zero-shot MedSigLIP and the same CNN architecture trained with Adam.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six MedMNIST tasks, mean test AUC was 0.719 for Opus and 0.711 for Astra versus 0.828 with 256 labelled training images; on SynthUterus, AUCs were 0.764 and 0.136, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Astra’s below-chance pelvic MRI result, attributed to a systematic error, highlights the need for task-specific validation before any clinical consideration.
infographic.paper_title: Weight-Space Programming for Medical Imaging: Do We Still Need Training Data?

title: AI in the Clinical Documentation Loop: Effects of LLM-Induced Note Bloat and Diagnostic Overcall on Downstream LLMs
authors: Jinghui Liu, Anthony Nguyen, Taylan Gurgenci
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to process medical records for healthcare tasks such as clinical documentation. Because these tools also generate documentation, the relationship is now bidirectional: models both read from and write to the record. Understanding how LLMs behave when reading records that already contain LLM-authored content is therefore critical for their safe deployment. In this study, we examine how LLM-authored content in the medical record affects downstream LLMs that read the same record. We consider two types of LLM-induced artifacts: bloat, in which LLM-generated summaries accumulate in the record and change the length and provenance of its content over time; and distortion, in which LLMs subtly alter clinical findings rather than fabricating facts outright. As a case of distortion, we study diagnostic overcall (documenting an unconfirmed differential diagnosis in the record) and test whether it propagates to the reader LLM's output. Across seven reader models from four families, we find evidence of both effects. First, LLM-generated summary notes modestly but consistently degraded downstream hospital-course generation compared with copy-forward and templated text of matched length. Second, injected overcalls reappeared in downstream outputs at rates that varied by reader model, without detectable changes in standard quality metrics. These findings show the need to monitor AI-generated content in medical records and to account for it when those records are later processed by AI.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-generated note bloat modestly reduced downstream summary quality, while diagnostic overcalls propagated into later LLM outputs without detectable changes in standard quality metrics.
infographic.clinical_relevance: AI-assisted documentation can influence later AI-generated summaries, making the origin and certainty of recorded information important to track.
method: Evaluated seven reader models from four model families on downstream hospital-course generation.
Compared accumulated LLM summaries with copy-forward and templated text of matched length.
Injected unconfirmed differential diagnoses and tested whether reader models repeated them.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the tested models, LLM summaries modestly but consistently degraded downstream generation, and overcall repetition varied by reader model.
infographic.watch_item: Standard quality metrics may miss propagated diagnostic overcalls; the abstract does not establish effects on patient outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: AI in the Clinical Documentation Loop: Effects of LLM-Induced Note Bloat and Diagnostic Overcall on Downstream LLMs

title: Decisions by Discrimination: Differential Evidence for Medical Reasoning
authors: Yunpeng Xiao, Yuzhang Xie, Junhao Huang, Carl Yang, Xiao Hu, Kai Shu
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly studied for clinical decision support, and medical question answering provides a testbed for evaluating this capability. In particular, medical multiple-choice questions (MCQs) reflect a core challenge in clinical decision-making: plausible options often share overlapping evidence, while only a few decisive factors distinguish the correct option from incorrect ones. However, existing retrieval-based and reasoning-oriented methods mainly focus on supplying broadly relevant knowledge or eliciting reasoning paths, rather than identifying the compact differential evidence that separates confusing alternatives. In this work, we present a retrieval-grounded differential evidence framework for medical MCQs. Our method extracts option-specific pieces of differential evidence and organizes them into concise evidence prompts for answer selection. This design better aligns external knowledge with differential reasoning while reducing irrelevant context. Experiments show consistent accuracy gains across multiple datasets and target LLMs. Ablation studies further show that our framework outperforms both directly using retrieved evidence chunks and closed-source LLM-generated general hints, and that its improvements are not solely explained by answer-proximal guidance, but are consistent with differential evidence serving as a compact aid for reasoning over competing alternatives. Our findings also offer insights for medical reasoning and other decision-making settings with multiple possible choices.

infographic.key_insight: Compact evidence that distinguishes competing answer options improved LLM accuracy on medical multiple-choice questions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach may inform clinical decision-support research by emphasizing evidence that separates plausible alternatives, but clinical utility remains unproven.
method: Retrieve external knowledge relevant to medical multiple-choice questions.
Extract option-specific evidence that distinguishes confusing alternatives.
Organize differential evidence into concise prompts for answer selection.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent accuracy gains across multiple datasets and target LLMs, with ablations outperforming retrieved chunks and closed-source LLM-generated general hints, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Medical question-answering performance does not establish safety or effectiveness in real clinical workflows.
infographic.paper_title: Decisions by Discrimination: Differential Evidence for Medical Reasoning

title: A local language model layered with rule-based and neural detectors for clinical text de-identification: an open-source toolkit and evaluation
authors: Valentin Burkin
abstract: Objectives: To measure whether a locally hosted large language model (LLM), stacked with deterministic and clinical named-entity recognition (NER) detectors, finds more protected health information (PHI) than open tools, and at what precision. Materials and Methods: DeidSharp, an open-source .NET toolkit, combines the findings of pluggable detectors (patterns, a clinical NER model, a local 26B mixture-of-experts LLM) and fails closed on any detector error. Configurations fixed on tuning halves were compared, under a prespecified protocol, with deid, Philter, the Stanford/Penn de-identifier, OpenAI Privacy Filter and GLiNER on reporting halves of PhysioNet's nursing notes (889 spans) and semi-synthetic MIMIC-IV-Note discharge summaries (29,023 spans), and on synthetic ASQ-PHI queries, with paired patient-level bootstrap intervals. Results: In the nursing notes, against Stanford/Penn, the recall-first stack found 98.9% of PHI (+2.8, 95% CI 1.4 to 4.4) at 9.3 points lower precision; the precision-first stack, without NER, found 96.5%, matching Stanford/Penn, at 19.6 points higher precision (83.2%). In the discharge summaries, both stacks led Stanford/Penn by more than 20 points (recall-first 95.3%, +21.5, 20.5 to 22.4), almost entirely on generated untyped names; on typed labels all three exceeded 99%. All four prespecified comparisons held. No configuration beat deid significantly on its home corpus; Philter found more discharge-summary spans than the recall-first stack at 23 points lower precision. Discussion: The LLM was the main detector and NER added place names; asked to verify its own findings, the LLM discarded a quarter of true PHI. Conclusion: A local LLM layered with deterministic detectors offers recall-first and precision-first operating points without sending text off-site.

infographic.key_insight: A locally hosted LLM layered with other detectors offered recall-first and precision-first options for identifying protected health information (PHI) without sending text off-site.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The toolkit could support privacy-preserving reuse of clinical text, but its missed-PHI and over-redaction trade-offs require local validation.
method: Combined rule-based detectors, clinical named-entity recognition (NER), and a local 26B mixture-of-experts LLM.
Evaluated recall-first and precision-first configurations against five de-identification tools.
Fixed configurations on tuning halves and evaluated reporting halves using paired patient-level bootstrap intervals.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across nursing notes (889 PHI spans) and semi-synthetic discharge summaries (29,023 spans), recall-first sensitivity reached 98.9% and 95.3%, respectively; all four prespecified comparisons held.
infographic.watch_item: The discharge-summary advantage over Stanford/Penn arose almost entirely from generated untyped names, limiting inference about performance on real-world clinical names.
infographic.paper_title: A local language model layered with rule-based and neural detectors for clinical text de-identification: an open-source toolkit and evaluation

title: Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus Task-Specific Training
authors: Emre Kutlusan, Yongmin Li
abstract: Foundation models pretrained on large natural-image collections are increasingly adapted for medical image segmentation, in the expectation that they will replace models trained for each task. Most comparisons, however, use data from the training distribution and a single task-specific baseline whose configuration is rarely justified, and therefore provide limited evidence of performance at new clinical sites. It also remains unclear how much of a foundation model must be adapted, and what determines this. We adapted a foundation model, DINOv2, with strategies ranging from tuning only its bias terms to full fine-tuning, and compared it with U-Nets and ResU-Nets trained from scratch. Experiments covered colonoscopy, breast ultrasound and dermoscopy, with testing on held-out data from the training source and on independent datasets from other institutions. The adapted foundation model generalised better on every external dataset. Within the training distribution, the task-specific models remained competitive when training data were abundant, and delineated boundaries more precisely, while the foundation model more often missed small lesions. Only a small fraction of the foundation model required adaptation, and the capacity needed was determined by the imaging domain rather than by the adaptation method. A widely used polyp test set was also found to duplicate images from another benchmark. Foundation-model adaptation is therefore warranted where models must work across sites, with capacity selected on the target domain.

infographic.key_insight: Adapted DINOv2 outperformed task-specific models on every external dataset tested, while models trained from scratch remained competitive within the training distribution when data were abundant.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Foundation-model adaptation may improve segmentation across clinical sites, but missed small lesions and less precise boundaries remain important concerns.
method: Adapted DINOv2 using strategies from bias-only tuning to full fine-tuning.
Compared against U-Nets and ResU-Nets trained from scratch.
Evaluated colonoscopy, breast ultrasound and dermoscopy segmentation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation included held-out source data and independent datasets from other institutions; only a small fraction of DINOv2 required adaptation, with capacity needs varying by imaging domain.
infographic.watch_item: Duplicate images were found across two polyp benchmarks, highlighting the need to audit dataset overlap when interpreting performance.
infographic.paper_title: Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus Task-Specific Training

title: The Dark Matter of Clinical Data: An Identification Limit on Disentangling Physiology from Care Process in electronic health records
authors: Mohammad Shahin, Krittaphas Chaisutyakorn, Dimitrios Proios, David Restrepo, Vishala Mishra, Boya Zhang
abstract: Representations learned from electronic health record (EHR) data encode patient physiology together with the clinical process that decides what is measured, when, and for whom. We formalize the data-generating process with latent physiology, ordering intent, laboratory values that exist only when measured, a learned representation, and clinical environments, and analyze two strategies for undoing this entanglement. First, no division of the information carried by laboratory "value" and "ordering" channels is identified from a single dataset: when ordering depends on the analyte, its distribution among untested patients is not recoverable, and a sentinel code for the undefined recorded value makes it carry all the entropy of the ordering indicator, fixing partial information decomposition (PID) for every redundancy measure satisfying the Williams-Beer axioms and invariant under injective re-encoding. Second, cross-site invariance of representation-conditional outcomes is a falsifiable implication of biological invariance taken jointly with exclusion and representation-sufficiency conditions, but not an identification strategy: we construct observationally equivalent models that disagree about biological invariance, whether the invariance test fails or passes. For binary physiology this happens exactly when case mix differs, the representation is lossy, and physiology affects the outcome. A worked example yields a 9.6-percentage-point cross-site gap under an unchanged biological mechanism. Tests performed for every patient remove the ordering gate, and measured tests can restore identification: biological invariance is identified when a test exactly summarizes outcome-relevant physiology, or, for binary physiology, when two tests with independent errors are available at sites with different case mix. Cross-site analyses should be reported as tests of a stated joint hypothesis.

infographic.key_insight: EHR representations entangle patient physiology with care processes, and neither a single dataset nor cross-site outcome invariance alone can identify their separate contributions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Differences in EHR-based predictions across hospitals may reflect testing practices and patient mix rather than changes in underlying biology.
method: Formalized latent physiology, test ordering, recorded laboratory values, representations, and clinical environments.
Used information-theoretic analysis and observationally equivalent models to establish identification limits.
Derived conditions under which universally measured tests or independent-error tests restore identification.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical results and a worked example showing a 9.6-percentage-point cross-site gap despite unchanged biology, rather than clinical validation.
infographic.watch_item: Report cross-site invariance analyses as tests of a joint hypothesis about biology, exclusion, and representation sufficiency—not as proof of biological invariance.
infographic.paper_title: The Dark Matter of Clinical Data: An Identification Limit on Disentangling Physiology from Care Process in electronic health records

title: Generative Active Learning for Label-Efficient Pan-Organ Ultrasound Diagnosis
authors: Yaofei Duan, Yuhao Huang, Yuan Gao, Ruixiang Qi, Tianyu Zhang, Yanlin Geng
abstract: Medical ultrasound (US) enables real-time, non-invasive diagnosis, yet building US-based AI systems is limited by data scarcity, costly expert annotation, and limited cross-center generalizability. Privacy constraints and instance-level reporting hinder the collection of diverse abnormal cases and frame-level labels, while repeated retraining for new centers increases computational cost. We introduce EvoDiff, a generative active learning framework that integrates diffusion modelling with information-theoretic objectives, evolutionary search, and curriculum-based sampling to select informative samples across heterogeneous US datasets. EvoDiff formulates sample selection as a generate-to-retrieve process, in which diffusion-based optimization in feature space guided by information gain produces synthetic probes, and only the real unlabeled samples retrieved by these probes are annotated and used for downstream training. Across six benchmarks covering fifteen datasets and 16,696 images, we evaluate EvoDiff on convolutional network and transformer-based foundation model. EvoDiff approaches fully supervised performance with substantially fewer labels, outperforms active learning baselines, and improves foundation model generalization under cross-domain external validation on unseen cohorts. A reader study with six radiologists indicates the potential to support clinical annotation workflows, with a model-based estimated 24% to 84% reduction in annotation workload at matched downstream performance.

infographic.key_insight: EvoDiff selects informative real ultrasound images for annotation, approaching fully supervised performance with substantially fewer labels.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could reduce expert annotation demands when developing ultrasound AI across organs and centers.
method: Combines diffusion modeling, information gain, evolutionary search, and curriculum-based sampling.
Generates synthetic feature-space probes to retrieve informative unlabeled images.
Uses only retrieved real images—not synthetic probes—for annotation and downstream training.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covered six benchmarks, 15 datasets, and 16,696 images using convolutional and transformer-based models; a six-radiologist reader study yielded model-based estimates of 24%–84% less annotation workload at matched downstream performance.
infographic.watch_item: Estimated annotation savings require prospective workflow validation and do not establish clinical diagnostic benefit.
infographic.paper_title: Generative Active Learning for Label-Efficient Pan-Organ Ultrasound Diagnosis

title: Application of Machine Learning and Deep Learning in diagnosis Covid19
authors: Merchi, L.; Boucheham, C.; Layeb, A.; Derouiche, A.
abstract: Predicting the progression of COVID-19 in hospitalised patients was an important challenge during the pandemic, particularly when healthcare resources were limited. This study investigates the use of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models to predict three clinical outcomes: death, admission to the intensive care unit (ICU), and clinical status (improvement or worsening). The study uses two patient datasets: an Algerian cohort of 80 patients from the Internal Medicine Department of the University Hospital Centre of Constantine, collected between July and August 2020, and a French cohort of 99 patients collected between March and May 2020. Five ML classifiers were evaluated: logistic regression (LR), k-nearest neighbours (KNN), classification and regression trees (CART), Naive Bayes (NB), and support vector machines (SVM). Their performance was examined in combination with three feature-selection methods: analysis of variance (ANOVA), mutual information (MI), and recursive feature elimination (RFE). The results were also compared with multilayer perceptron (MLP) models using one to five hidden layers. Model evaluation included 30 repetitions of five-fold cross-validation on the training data, followed by evaluation on a separate hold-out test set. The results showed that selecting 20 features generally provided better cross-validated accuracy than selecting 30 features or using the full feature set. The best-performing classifier-feature-selection combination varied across the six dataset-outcome tasks. LR combined with RFE was selected for three tasks, LR combined with ANOVA for one task, and CART combined with ANOVA for two tasks. The selected ML models achieved test-set accuracies ranging from 0.47 to 0.95 and higher accuracy than the average MLP results in five of the six tasks. These findings suggest that ML methods can be useful for exploring clinical outcomes in hospitalised COVID-19 patients. However, the small sample sizes and limitations of the available data mean that the results should be interpreted with caution. Further evaluation using larger and independent patient datasets is needed before these models can be considered for clinical use.

infographic.key_insight: Selected machine-learning models outperformed average multilayer perceptron results on five of six COVID-19 outcome-prediction tasks, but performance varied substantially.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These models explore prediction of death, ICU admission, and improvement or worsening in hospitalised COVID-19 patients, without establishing readiness for clinical use.
method: Compared five classifiers: logistic regression, KNN, CART, Naive Bayes, and SVM.
Tested ANOVA, mutual information, and recursive feature elimination; selecting 20 features generally improved cross-validated accuracy.
Compared selected classifiers with multilayer perceptrons using one to five hidden layers.
infographic.evidence_signal: Two cohorts—80 Algerian and 99 French patients—were evaluated using 30 repetitions of five-fold cross-validation and separate hold-out testing; selected ML models achieved test accuracies of 0.47–0.95.
infographic.watch_item: Small, early-pandemic cohorts limit generalisability; larger independent datasets are needed before clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: Application of Machine Learning and Deep Learning in diagnosis Covid19

title: Large Language Model-Enhanced Electronic Frailty Assessment and Prognostic Performance in Hospitalized Adults: A Retrospective Cohort Study
authors: Dalal, A. K.; Lundstedt, J.; Ernecoff, N.; Plombon, S.; Streiter, S.; Leeson, M.; Plasek, J.; Mueller, S.; Fiskio, J.; Zhou, L.; Lipsitz, S.; Orkaby, A.; Loewenthal, J.
abstract: BackgroundElectronic frailty indices (eFIs) derived from structured electronic health record (EHR) data may incompletely capture functional deficits. Large language models (LLMs) can extract frailty-related information from clinical notes, but whether improved frailty ascertainment improves prognostic performance is uncertain. ObjectiveTo compare frailty ascertainment and prognostic performance between standard and LLM-enhanced eFIs among hospitalized adults. DesignRetrospective cohort study ParticipantsAdults aged [≥]50 years enrolled in two studies at an academic medical center and affiliated community hospital between February 2022 and April 2024. Main MeasuresA validated 35-deficit diagnosis-based eFI and an LLM-enhanced eFI incorporating deficits extracted from physical therapy (PT) documentation using GPT-4o. Frailty was defined using an index threshold of [≥]0.20. The primary outcome was a composite of discharge to a facility, readmission, or death within 90 days. Multivariable logistic regression models assessed associations with the outcome, and discrimination was compared using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Secondary analyses examined threshold-based classification and PT-documentation availability; prespecified sensitivity analyses evaluated population and outcome restrictions. ResultsAmong 616 hospitalizations, mean (SD) age was 70.9 (10.2) years, 329 (53.4%) had PT documentation, and 320 (51.9%) experienced the composite outcome. Standard and LLM-enhanced eFIs classified 216 (35.1%) and 362 (58.8%) hospitalizations as frail, respectively. Both were independently associated with the outcome (standard eFI: adjusted OR, 1.98 [95% CI, 1.39-2.83]; LLM-enhanced eFI: adjusted OR, 2.46 [95% CI, 1.75-3.47]). Discrimination did not differ significantly (AUROC, 0.636 vs 0.660; difference, 0.024 [95% CI, -0.006 to 0.053]; p=0.12). LLM enhancement increased sensitivity (42.5% to 69.4%) but decreased specificity (73.0% to 52.7%). ConclusionsLLM enhancement substantially increased frailty ascertainment and sensitivity for adverse outcomes but did not significantly improve prognostic discrimination. Thus, LLM-enhanced frailty assessment may depend on whether the intended use prioritizes broad identification of functional vulnerability or prediction of adverse post-hospital outcomes.

infographic.key_insight: Adding GPT-4o–extracted deficits from physical therapy notes increased frailty identification but did not significantly improve prognostic discrimination.
infographic.clinical_relevance: LLM-enhanced frailty assessment identified more hospitalizations associated with adverse outcomes, with higher sensitivity but lower specificity than the standard index.
method: Retrospective cohort of 616 hospitalizations among adults aged ≥50 years at two affiliated hospitals.
Compared a validated 35-deficit electronic frailty index with an enhanced version incorporating GPT-4o–extracted deficits.
Evaluated associations and AUROC for discharge to a facility, readmission, or death within 90 days.
infographic.evidence_signal: Frailty classification increased from 35.1% to 58.8% and sensitivity from 42.5% to 69.4%, while specificity fell from 73.0% to 52.7%; AUROC increased from 0.636 to 0.660 without statistical significance (p=0.12).
infographic.watch_item: Physical therapy documentation was available for only 53.4% of hospitalizations, potentially limiting the consistency of LLM enhancement.
infographic.paper_title: Large Language Model-Enhanced Electronic Frailty Assessment and Prognostic Performance in Hospitalized Adults: A Retrospective Cohort Study

title: Toward Foundation Detection Models via Example-Based Grounding in EM-DETR
authors: Sheethal Bhat, Bogdan Georgescu, Awais Mansoor, Florin C. Ghesu, Sasa Grbic, Andreas Maier
abstract: DeepLearning (DL)-based Computer-Aided Diagnostic (CAD) systems have shown great promise in supporting clinicians, but their performance heavily depends on the availability of large, well-annotated datasets. In medical lesion detection, the scarcity of comprehensive, stan dardized annotations and the heterogeneity of existing datasets limit the development of robust foundation models. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to building a multi-domain foundation model for le sion detection by integrating diverse medical image datasets annotated for both anatomical structures and abnormalities. We first propose a student-teacher training strategy to effectively combine datasets with heterogeneous label spaces, mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and im proving feature learning. In addition, building on our previously pro posed example-based EM-DETR framework, we adapt it to jointly learn from multiple domain-specific datasets, enabling fine-grained, example driven detection across modalities. Our model achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results, with image-level AUC scores exceeding previous SOTA by 1% point on four key findings in CXRs. We achieve a leading mAP50 in CXRs and mammography, surpassing EM-DETR trained on a single dataset by 2-3% points. This approach paves the way for scalable foundation models in medical imaging that leverage heterogeneous data while maintaining robust and generalizable performance.

infographic.key_insight: EM-DETR combines heterogeneous medical imaging datasets with example-based grounding to improve multi-domain lesion detection.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support more adaptable computer-aided detection across chest X-rays and mammography, but clinical benefit remains unestablished.
method: Integrates datasets annotated for anatomical structures and abnormalities.
Uses student–teacher training to reconcile heterogeneous labels and mitigate catastrophic forgetting.
Extends example-based EM-DETR for joint learning across domain-specific datasets.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports image-level AUC gains exceeding 1 percentage point over prior state of the art for four chest X-ray findings and mAP50 gains of 2–3 percentage points over single-dataset EM-DETR in chest X-rays and mammography.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify dataset sizes, external validation, or prospective clinical evaluation, limiting assessment of real-world generalizability.
infographic.paper_title: Toward Foundation Detection Models via Example-Based Grounding in EM-DETR

title: DuSS-PET: Self-Supervised Low-Dose PET Reconstruction Using Pseudo-Dual-Domain Consistency Without Paired Data
authors: Shuijin Lin, Yuzhu He, Yongbo Wang, Jianhua Ma, Fan Wang
abstract: Positron emission tomography (PET) is pivotal in medicine and healthcare, but requires high radiation doses for quality imaging. Although deep learning has shown promise for low-dose PET reconstruction/enhancement, existing methods primarily rely on fully supervised learning, which requires paired low- and full-dose scans that are clinically impractical to obtain. To overcome this fundamental limitation, we propose DuSS-PET, a novel self-supervised PET reconstruction framework that operates without any paired low- and full-dose data. Our method is built upon a computational Noisier2Noise (Nr2N) paradigm, featuring a Bernoulli corruption strategy that serves as an image-space approximation to emulate low-count noise patterns in image-derived pseudo-sinogram representations. The DuSS-PET framework integrates three core components: an adaptive Swin transformer for pseudo-sinogram restoration, a plug-and-play module for image enhancement, and a consistency-constrained SSL strategy that enforces agreement between the pseudo-sinogram and image representations. Extensive experiments on multi-center datasets demonstrate that DuSS-PET achieves superior reconstruction performance, outperforming state-of-the-art SSL methods and achieving comparable or even better results than fully supervised approaches across various dose levels. In particular, it exhibits exceptional generalization across different scanner vendors. This work is among the first self-supervised low-dose PET reconstruction framework that enforces consistency between reconstructed images and pseudo-sinograms, where the pseudo-sinogram generated in the image space serves as a solid computational consistency constraint for enhanced imaging without full-dose training scans. The source code will be publicly available at https://github.com/ladderlab-xjtu/DuSS-PET.

infographic.key_insight: DuSS-PET reconstructs low-dose PET images without paired low- and full-dose training scans by enforcing consistency between images and image-derived pseudo-sinograms.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support lower-dose PET imaging while reducing reliance on paired training data, but clinical utility remains to be established.
method: Uses computational Noisier2Noise training with Bernoulli corruption to approximate low-count noise.
Combines adaptive Swin transformer pseudo-sinogram restoration with plug-and-play image enhancement.
Enforces self-supervised consistency between image and pseudo-sinogram representations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports multi-center evaluation across dose levels and scanner vendors, outperforming other self-supervised methods and matching or exceeding fully supervised approaches, without providing quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Image-derived pseudo-sinograms approximate acquisition data; preservation of quantitative PET measurements and diagnostic findings requires clinical validation.
infographic.paper_title: DuSS-PET: Self-Supervised Low-Dose PET Reconstruction Using Pseudo-Dual-Domain Consistency Without Paired Data
